lines.text: In fourteen ninety-eight,
three small ships dropped anchor off the coast of Kerala.
Their crews had sailed for almost eleven months,
all the way around Africa,
for one thing: pepper.
They had just started a story
that would last four hundred and sixty-three years.
Chapter one. The Spice Problem.
In fourteen fifty-three,
the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople,
and the old roads to the East fell into other hands.
Indian pepper, silk and cotton still reached Europe,
but only through Arab middlemen,
and every one of them took a cut.
So little Portugal, on the edge of the Atlantic,
made a bold bet:
if you can't go through, go around.
Prince Henry, the Navigator,
pushed ship after ship down the coast of Africa,
and in fourteen eighty-eight, Bartholomew Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope.
The door to the Indian Ocean was open.
Chapter two. Hello, Kalikut.
Ten years later, Vasco da Gama walked through it.
In East Africa, he picked up a Gujarati pilot
who knew the monsoon winds,
and in May fourteen ninety-eight, he reached Kalikut.
Kalikut's Hindu king, the Zam-oh-rin,
grew rich by welcoming traders,
so he welcomed this one too.
The Arab merchants were far less happy.
For centuries, Indians, Arabs, Africans and Chinese
had shared this ocean by unwritten rules:
everyone traded, but nobody owned the sea.
The Portuguese wanted to own it.
Da Gama sailed home with a cargo worth a fortune,
because pepper that cost little in Kerala
sold for many times as much in Europe.
Chapter three. Traders Become Raiders.
The next fleet, under Pedro Cabral,
set up a trading post in Kalikut in fifteen hundred.
Locals attacked it,
and several Portuguese died.
Cabral struck back:
he burned Arab ships in the harbour
and turned his cannons on the city.
Then he sailed south, and made friends with Kalikut's rivals,
Cochin and Kanna-nore.
When da Gama returned,
and demanded that the Zam-oh-rin expel every Arab trader,
the Zam-oh-rin refused,
and the trading posts quietly grew walls and guns.
In fifteen-oh-three, the first Portuguese fort rose at Cochin.
Chapter four. Rule the Water.
In fifteen-oh-five, Portugal sent its first governor,
Francisco de Al-may-da, with a simple plan:
forget the land, control the water.
Every ship now needed a Portuguese pass,
or risked being seized.
That threatened Gujarat, Egypt,
and even the merchants of Venice,
so Egypt and Gujarat joined forces.
In fifteen-oh-eight, at Chowl, they beat the Portuguese,
and Al-may-da's own son was killed.
A year later, off Dee-oo,
Al-may-da destroyed their fleet.
His lesson was clear:
whoever rules the sea holds India.
Chapter five. Al-boo-kerk's Goa.
His successor, Afonso de Al-boo-kerk, went further.
He built strongholds at every gate of the ocean,
from Hor-mooz to Muh-lakka,
and in fifteen-ten, he captured Goa from the Sultan of Bee-jah-poor.
He told his men to marry local women and settle down.
They brought tobacco and cashew,
and Al-boo-kerk banned sati in Goa.
But Muslims, Portugal's old rivals,
were bitterly persecuted.
By fifteen-thirty, Goa was the capital,
and in fifteen thirty-seven, Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
went aboard a Portuguese ship for talks,
and never came home.
Chapter six. Priests and Emperors.
In fifteen-eighty, two Jesuit priests from Goa
reached the court of Emperor Akbar,
who loved debating religion.
The Portuguese dreamed that if the emperor converted,
Mughal India would follow.
He didn't.
Back in Goa, after the Inquisition arrived,
Hindus were persecuted too.
Then, in sixteen-oh-eight, an Englishman, William Hawkins,
landed at Surat with a letter from his king.
The Portuguese tried everything to stop him,
but in sixteen twelve, English ships beat a Portuguese fleet near Surat,
and Emperor Jahangir, who had no navy, was impressed.
Chapter seven. The Fall.
The worst blow came in Bengal.
At Hoog-lee, Portuguese traders ran a cruel slave trade,
seizing Hindu and Muslim children,
and, chroniclers say, even took two slave girls of Empress Mum-taz Mahal.
In sixteen thirty-two, Shah Jahan's army besieged Hoog-lee,
and three months later, the Portuguese were gone from Bengal.
Everything else was slipping too.
Portugal's crown had passed to Spain,
dragging it into Spain's wars,
Brazil was now worth more than India,
and the sea route was no longer a secret.
By sixteen sixty-three, the Dutch had taken every Portuguese fort on the Malabar coast.
In seventeen thirty-nine, the Marathas took Bassein.
One Portuguese governor put it best:
they came with a sword in one hand and a cross in the other,
filled their pockets with gold,
and grew too heavy to hold either.
Chapter eight. Last to Leave.
And yet, Goa, Duh-mun and Dee-oo stayed Portuguese.
They outlasted the Mughals, the Marathas, even the British.
Only in nineteen sixty-one did India take them back,
four hundred and sixty-three years after da Gama reached Kalikut.
The first Europeans to arrive
were the last to leave.
And it all began with three small ships,
and a taste for pepper.
